<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:神道政治連盟]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11590929]] Wikidata name: Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:23, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox organization | name = Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership | image = Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership.jpg | caption = | headquarters = {{JPN}} | location = Yoyogi 1-1-2, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo (inside the Association of Shinto Shrines)<ref name="sinseiren">{{Cite web|date= |url=https://www.sinseiren.org/ |title=See each section for details |publisher=Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref> | leader_title = President | leader_name = Fumihiro Uchida<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-06-12 |url=https://diamond.jp/articles/-/240074 |title=Shinto Political Federation Leader Commits Suicide Amidst Criminal Accusation Movement |publisher=DIAMOND online |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref> | established = November 8, 1969<ref name="yakuwae-1970-03-27"/> | affiliated = [[Shinto Political Federation Diet Members' Alliance]] | website = https://www.sinseiren.org/ }}
The ''''''Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership'''''' ({{lang-ja|神道政治連盟}}, ''Shintō Seiji Renmei''), abbreviated as '''Shinseiren''' (神政連), is a political organization in Japan. Established on November 8, 1969, it serves as the lobbying arm of the [[:en:Association of Shinto Shrines|Association of Shinto Shrines]], representing Shinto-affiliated interests.<ref>{{Cite web|date= |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/jinjahoncho/concerned |title=List of Related Organizations |publisher=Association of Shinto Shrines |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref>
== Overview == [[File:Jinja-Honcho-1966-2.png|thumb|160px|First President Kazue Uesugi]] Shinseiren is composed of members from the Shinto community. Its stated mission is to "properly convey Japan's traditions and culture to future generations" and to "restore Japanese identity and pride through movements such as constitutional revision, based on the spirit of Shinto." It maintains headquarters in every Japanese prefecture, with its central office located within the Association of Shinto Shrines in Yoyogi, Shibuya, Tokyo.
Following recommendations from the 1966 Shinto Council, the preparatory committee proposed the establishment of Shinseiren. While an early goal was to elect priests to the House of Councillors, it later shifted focus to supporting Shinto-affiliated candidates from existing political parties.<ref>{{Sfn|塚田穂高|2015|pp=36-49}}</ref> Shinseiren formally launched on November 8, 1969, with Kazue Uesugi as its first president.<ref name="yakuwae-1970-03-27">{{cite web | url=http://www.tokyo-shinsei.jp/yakuwae/yakuwae-sokan.pdf | title=‘Yakuwai’ Inaugural Issue (Published March 27, 1970) | publisher=Tokyo Shinto Youth Association | date= | accessdate=2024-1-9 }}</ref>
In its founding charter, Shinseiren outlined its objectives, including research on political issues, public education, publishing activities, and supporting candidates for political office through elections.<ref>{{Sfn|神道政治連盟|1984|pp=153-154}}</ref> Membership is open to individuals and organizations over 20 years old who align with the association’s mission.
== Connection with Nippon Kaigi == The organization has close ties with [[:en:Nippon Kaigi|Nippon Kaigi]], a conservative nationalist group established in 1997.<ref>{{cite news |last= Mesmer |first= Philippe |url= https://www.lemonde.fr/asie-pacifique/article/2016/08/03/a-tokyo-une-nationaliste-nommee-a-la-defense_4977923_3216.html | title= A nationalist appointed to Japan's Ministry of Defense | newspaper= Le Monde | date= 2016-8-3 |accessdate= 2021-1-19 }}</ref> Many of Shinseiren’s leaders also serve as officers in Nippon Kaigi.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nipponkaigi.org/about/yakuin | title=Executive List (as of July 1, 2022) | publisher=Nippon Kaigi | date= | accessdate=2024-1-10 }}</ref> Despite their similarities, Shinseiren primarily acts as an electoral support group, while Nippon Kaigi engages in broader ideological advocacy.<ref>{{Cite web|author=高野孟|date=2015-07-14 |url=https://www.mag2.com/p/money/4237/2 |title=The Hidden Goals of Shinseiren and Nippon Kaigi |publisher=MONEY VOICE |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref>
== Activities and Advocacy == Shinseiren promotes the following initiatives:<ref name="sinseiren" /> * Drafting a new constitution, with a focus on revising postwar policies and restoring "distorted national values." * Official state recognition of rituals for spirits enshrined at [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]]. * Maintenance of the male imperial line and opposition to {{ill|female-headed imperial branches|ja|女性宮家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/female-headed imperial branches|qq=}}. * Denial of the {{ill|International Military Tribunal for the Far East|lt=Tokyo Trials|ja|極東国際軍事裁判|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/International Military Tribunal for the Far East|1=International Military Tribunal for the Far East|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q320680}} and the depiction of Japan's wars as efforts to "liberate Asia." * Promotion of traditional moral values through the revival of the {{ill|Imperial Rescript on Education|ja|教育勅語|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Rescript on Education|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 教育ニ関スル勅語}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sinseiren.org/info_details70.html |title=New Leaflet on the Imperial Rescript on Education |publisher=Shinseiren |date=2020-10-30}}</ref>
== Role in Elections == Shinseiren supports candidates for the House of Councillors who align with its values, such as respect for the imperial family, constitutional revision, and opposition to liberal reforms like gender equality initiatives.
== Key Supported Candidates: == * '''2001''': Haruko Arimura, Hidenobu Otsuji, Shin Sakurai * '''2016''': Eriko Yamatani * '''2019''': Haruko Arimura<ref>{{Sfn|塚田穂高|2015|pp=68-69}}</ref>
== External Links == * [Official website](https://www.sinseiren.org/)

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:神道政治連盟]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11590929]] Wikidata name: Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:23, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox organization | name = Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership | image = Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership.jpg | caption = | headquarters = {{JPN}} | location = Yoyogi 1-1-2, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo (inside the Association of Shinto Shrines)<ref name="sinseiren">{{Cite web|date= |url=https://www.sinseiren.org/ |title=See each section for details |publisher=Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref> | leader_title = President | leader_name = Fumihiro Uchida<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-06-12 |url=https://diamond.jp/articles/-/240074 |title=Shinto Political Federation Leader Commits Suicide Amidst Criminal Accusation Movement |publisher=DIAMOND online |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref> | established = November 8, 1969<ref name="yakuwae-1970-03-27"/> | affiliated = [[Shinto Political Federation Diet Members' Alliance]] | website = https://www.sinseiren.org/ }}
The ''''''Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership'''''' ({{lang-ja|神道政治連盟}}, ''Shintō Seiji Renmei''), abbreviated as '''Shinseiren''' (神政連), is a political organization in Japan. Established on November 8, 1969, it serves as the lobbying arm of the [[:en:Association of Shinto Shrines|Association of Shinto Shrines]], representing Shinto-affiliated interests.<ref>{{Cite web|date= |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/jinjahoncho/concerned |title=List of Related Organizations |publisher=Association of Shinto Shrines |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref>
== Overview == [[File:Jinja-Honcho-1966-2.png|thumb|160px|First President Kazue Uesugi]] Shinseiren is composed of members from the Shinto community. Its stated mission is to "properly convey Japan's traditions and culture to future generations" and to "restore Japanese identity and pride through movements such as constitutional revision, based on the spirit of Shinto." It maintains headquarters in every Japanese prefecture, with its central office located within the Association of Shinto Shrines in Yoyogi, Shibuya, Tokyo.
Following recommendations from the 1966 Shinto Council, the preparatory committee proposed the establishment of Shinseiren. While an early goal was to elect priests to the House of Councillors, it later shifted focus to supporting Shinto-affiliated candidates from existing political parties.<ref>{{Sfn|塚田穂高|2015|pp=36-49}}</ref> Shinseiren formally launched on November 8, 1969, with Kazue Uesugi as its first president.<ref name="yakuwae-1970-03-27">{{cite web | url=http://www.tokyo-shinsei.jp/yakuwae/yakuwae-sokan.pdf | title=‘Yakuwai’ Inaugural Issue (Published March 27, 1970) | publisher=Tokyo Shinto Youth Association | date= | accessdate=2024-1-9 }}</ref>
In its founding charter, Shinseiren outlined its objectives, including research on political issues, public education, publishing activities, and supporting candidates for political office through elections.<ref>{{Sfn|神道政治連盟|1984|pp=153-154}}</ref> Membership is open to individuals and organizations over 20 years old who align with the association’s mission.
== Connection with Nippon Kaigi == The organization has close ties with [[:en:Nippon Kaigi|Nippon Kaigi]], a conservative nationalist group established in 1997.<ref>{{cite news |last= Mesmer |first= Philippe |url= https://www.lemonde.fr/asie-pacifique/article/2016/08/03/a-tokyo-une-nationaliste-nommee-a-la-defense_4977923_3216.html | title= A nationalist appointed to Japan's Ministry of Defense | newspaper= Le Monde | date= 2016-8-3 |accessdate= 2021-1-19 }}</ref> Many of Shinseiren’s leaders also serve as officers in Nippon Kaigi.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nipponkaigi.org/about/yakuin | title=Executive List (as of July 1, 2022) | publisher=Nippon Kaigi | date= | accessdate=2024-1-10 }}</ref> Despite their similarities, Shinseiren primarily acts as an electoral support group, while Nippon Kaigi engages in broader ideological advocacy.<ref>{{Cite web|author=高野孟|date=2015-07-14 |url=https://www.mag2.com/p/money/4237/2 |title=The Hidden Goals of Shinseiren and Nippon Kaigi |publisher=MONEY VOICE |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref>
== Activities and Advocacy == Shinseiren promotes the following initiatives:<ref name="sinseiren" /> * Drafting a new constitution, with a focus on revising postwar policies and restoring "distorted national values." * Official state recognition of rituals for spirits enshrined at [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]]. * Maintenance of the male imperial line and opposition to {{ill|female-headed imperial branches|ja|女性宮家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/female-headed imperial branches|qq=}}. * Denial of the {{ill|International Military Tribunal for the Far East|lt=Tokyo Trials|ja|極東国際軍事裁判|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/International Military Tribunal for the Far East|1=International Military Tribunal for the Far East|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q320680}} and the depiction of Japan's wars as efforts to "liberate Asia." * Promotion of traditional moral values through the revival of the {{ill|Imperial Rescript on Education|ja|教育勅語|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Rescript on Education|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 教育ニ関スル勅語}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sinseiren.org/info_details70.html |title=New Leaflet on the Imperial Rescript on Education |publisher=Shinseiren |date=2020-10-30}}</ref>
== Role in Elections == Shinseiren supports candidates for the House of Councillors who align with its values, such as respect for the imperial family, constitutional revision, and opposition to liberal reforms like gender equality initiatives.
== Key Supported Candidates: == * '''2001''': Haruko Arimura, Hidenobu Otsuji, Shin Sakurai * '''2016''': Eriko Yamatani * '''2019''': Haruko Arimura<ref>{{Sfn|塚田穂高|2015|pp=68-69}}</ref>
== External Links == * [Official website](https://www.sinseiren.org/)

It maintains headquarters in every Japanese prefecture, with its central office located within the Association of Shinto Shrines in Yoyogi, Shibuya, Tokyo.
Following recommendations from the 1966 Shinto Council, the preparatory committee proposed the establishment of Shinseiren. While an early goal was to elect priests to the House of Councillors, it later shifted focus to supporting Shinto-affiliated candidates from existing political parties.<ref>{{Sfn|塚田穂高|2015|pp=36-49}}</ref> Shinseiren formally launched on November 8, 1969, with Kazue Uesugi as its first president.<ref name="yakuwae-1970-03-27">{{cite web | url=http://www.tokyo-shinsei.jp/yakuwae/yakuwae-sokan.pdf | title=‘Yakuwai’ Inaugural Issue (Published March 27, 1970) | publisher=Tokyo Shinto Youth Association | date= | accessdate=2024-1-9 }}</ref>
In its founding charter, Shinseiren outlined its objectives, including research on political issues, public education, publishing activities, and supporting candidates for political office through elections.<ref>{{Sfn|神道政治連盟|1984|pp=153-154}}</ref> Membership is open to individuals and organizations over 20 years old who align with the association’s mission.
== Connection with Nippon Kaigi == The organization has close ties with {{ill|Nippon Kaigi|en|Nippon Kaigi|WD=Q11507216|lt=Nippon Kaigi}}, a conservative nationalist group established in 1997.<ref>{{cite news |last= Mesmer |first= Philippe |url= https://www.lemonde.fr/asie-pacifique/article/2016/08/03/a-tokyo-une-nationaliste-nommee-a-la-defense_4977923_3216.html | title= A nationalist appointed to Japan's Ministry of Defense | newspaper= Le Monde | date= 2016-8-3 |accessdate= 2021-1-19 }}</ref> Many of Shinseiren’s leaders also serve as officers in Nippon Kaigi.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nipponkaigi.org/about/yakuin | title=Executive List (as of July 1, 2022) | publisher=Nippon Kaigi | date= | accessdate=2024-1-10 }}</ref> Despite their similarities, Shinseiren primarily acts as an electoral support group, while Nippon Kaigi engages in broader ideological advocacy.<ref>{{Cite web|author=高野孟|date=2015-07-14 |url=https://www.mag2.com/p/money/4237/2 |title=The Hidden Goals of Shinseiren and Nippon Kaigi |publisher=MONEY VOICE |accessdate=2020-12-20}}</ref>
== Activities and Advocacy == Shinseiren promotes the following initiatives:<ref name="sinseiren" /> * Drafting a new constitution, with a focus on revising postwar policies and restoring "distorted national values." * Official state recognition of rituals for spirits enshrined at {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine}}. * Maintenance of the male imperial line and opposition to {{ill|female-headed imperial branches|ja|女性宮家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/female-headed imperial branches|qq=}}. * Denial of the {{ill|International Military Tribunal for the Far East|lt=Tokyo Trials|ja|極東国際軍事裁判|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/International Military Tribunal for the Far East|1=International Military Tribunal for the Far East|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q320680}} and the depiction of Japan's wars as efforts to "liberate Asia." * Promotion of traditional moral values through the revival of the {{ill|Imperial Rescript on Education|ja|教育勅語|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Rescript on Education|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 教育ニ関スル勅語}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sinseiren.org/info_details70.html |title=New Leaflet on the Imperial Rescript on Education |publisher=Shinseiren |date=2020-10-30}}</ref>
== Role in Elections == Shinseiren supports candidates for the House of Councillors who align with its values, such as respect for the imperial family, constitutional revision, and opposition to liberal reforms like gender equality initiatives.
== Key Supported Candidates: == * '''2001''': Haruko Arimura, Hidenobu Otsuji, Shin Sakurai * '''2016''': Eriko Yamatani * '''2019''': Haruko Arimura<ref>{{Sfn|塚田穂高|2015|pp=68-69}}</ref>
== External Links == * [Official website](https://www.sinseiren.org/)
